title: Increasing, Decreasing and the First Derivative Test
short: The sign of f′ tells where f rises or falls.
trouble: Students find where f′ = 0 but never test the sign on each side.

blocks.html: The The Mean Value Theorem has an everyday consequence: the sign of the derivative tells where a function rises and falls. That turns finding peaks and valleys into reading a sign chart.

If $f' > 0$ on an interval, $f$ is increasing there; if $f' < 0$, decreasing. First derivative test: at a critical number $c$, if $f'$ changes from $+$ to $-$, $f$ has a local max; from $-$ to $+$, a local min; if $f'$ does not change sign, neither.

Take $x_1 < x_2$ in an interval where $f' > 0$. By the MVT, $f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1)$ for some $c$ between them. Both factors are positive, so $f(x_2) > f(x_1)$: the function increases. The test follows: rising then falling makes a peak; falling then rising makes a valley.

opts.task: The top graph is green where $f$ rises and red where it falls. Find where the color changes, and check what $f'$ does there.

items: Find the critical numbers and mark them on a number line.
Pick a test point in each piece and find the sign of $f'$ there (or use the signs of the factors).
Read off increasing and decreasing intervals, and classify each critical number.

blocks.title: A cubic
blocks.q: Find where $f(x) = \frac{x^3}{3} - x^2 - 3x$ increases and decreases, and classify its critical numbers.
steps: So $f$ increases on $(-\infty, -1)$ and $(3, \infty)$ and decreases on $(-1, 3)$.
$+ \to -$ at $-1$: local max. $- \to +$ at 3: local min.
blocks.a: Local max at $x = -1$, local min at $x = 3$.

blocks.title: A flat point that is not an extreme
blocks.q: Classify the critical numbers of $f(x) = x^4 - 4x^3$.
steps: $4x^2 \ge 0$, so the sign of $f'$ is the sign of $x - 3$: negative on both sides of 0, positive after 3.
At 0 the sign does not change: neither max nor min. At 3: $- \to +$, a local min.

blocks.html: Finding where $f' = 0$ and stopping there, calling every such point a max or min. The second example shows a flat point that is neither. Check: always test the sign of $f'$ on both sides of each critical number.
